short.headline: Net foreign direct investment collapsed, but gross inflows hit a record, the money did not flee, the arithmetic changed
short.dek: India’s net FDI dropped from $43 billion in FY20 to under $1 billion in FY25, but gross inflows surged to an all-time high of $81 billion. The gap is repatriation and Indian firms investing abroad.
short.body: Foreign money is not fleeing India. The panic comes from reading the net foreign direct investment figure as if it were gross. In FY2024-25, net FDI fell to just $about $1 billion, the lowest in years. But the same year, gross FDI inflows touched a record $$80.6 billion. The collapse in net was driven by money flowing out: repatriation of profits and disinvestment rose to $$51.5 billion, and outward investment by Indian companies climbed to $$28.2 billion. This is a story of a maturing market that pays profits home and Indian businesses that go global. Meanwhile, the hot money of portfolio flows swings wildly on global cues, not just local politics.

macha.heading: Okay, but what does this actually mean, macha?
macha.body: Picture this: your chai shop is doing great. The next year, you count the cash left after paying for milk and sugar, and it’s less. You panic, but the real reason is you’ve started giving your brother money to open his own tapri, and you paid back a loan with interest. That’s exactly what happened with India’s foreign investment numbers. The money coming in is still at a record high. It’s just that more of it is now going back out as profits, or as Indian companies buying firms abroad. So the headline ‘foreigners are leaving’ is backward. The money coming in is real; what’s new is how much is also going out. And the hot money that comes and goes? That’s driven more by what the US Federal Reserve does than by anything in Delhi.
macha.soWhat: India didn’t lose its foreign investor appeal; it gained a two-way street where money comes in, grows, and partly returns, just like a mature economy.

article.title: Is foreign money really fleeing India? What FDI and FII numbers actually mean.
article.standfirst: The number everyone quotes, net FDI, plunged. But gross inflows hit a record, and the gap was not foreigners leaving but repatriation and Indian firms going global. Here is how to read the real story.
article.bodyMarkdown:
The year-end headlines screamed a single number: net foreign direct investment fell to less than a billion dollars in 2024-25, down from 43 billion five years earlier. That sounds like a stampede. But it is not. The mistake is reading the net figure as if it were the gross. Foreign money is not fleeing India; the arithmetic of how we count it has changed. This is the real story, told chart by chart.

## Why does everyone think foreign money is fleeing India?

Because the chart looks terrifying. Net FDI, the money that stays after outflows, stood at $43 billion in 2019-20 and collapsed to about $1 billion in 2024-25. On a screen, that is a cliff. The number is real, it comes from the RBI’s balance of payments, and it is what every newsroom quotes. But net FDI is a subtraction. It is not the same as the fresh money foreigners bring in. To understand why the net number fell, you have to look at the taps and the drain separately, not just the water level in the bucket.

## What’s the difference between FDI and FII?

They are completely different animals. FDI, foreign direct investment, is money that buys lasting control. A foreign company sets up a factory, buys a 10 percent or larger stake in an Indian firm, and stays. It is patient money. FII, or more precisely FPI (foreign portfolio investment), is money that buys shares or bonds on the open market for a quick return. It can leave tomorrow. In the balance of payments, the country’s official ledger, they sit in separate columns and behave nothing like each other. Annual FDI moves like a steady march. Annual FII swings from plus $36.1 billion one year to minus $16.8 billion the next. You cannot read one like the other.

## If FDI ‘collapsed’, why did gross inflows hit a record?

Because the net number is a subtraction, not a reading on the inflow tap. In 2024-25, gross FDI into India reached $80.6 billion, the highest ever recorded. The same year, net FDI was about $1 billion. So foreigners came in record numbers. The gap between gross and net is the drain: the money that goes back out. And that drain swelled. The year the net figure ‘collapsed’, the inflow tap was running at full pressure. The crisis was not about money coming in; it was about money going out.

## Where did the missing net FDI go?

Two drains grew rapidly. The first is repatriation. When a foreign-owned company in India makes a profit, it sends some of that money home. When it sells its stake, the exit proceeds leave the country. Together, this repatriation and disinvestment surged from $18.4 billion in 2019-20 to $51.5 billion in 2024-25. The second drain is outward direct investment. Indian firms investing abroad, buying companies, building plants, climbed from $13 billion to $28.2 billion over the same period. Add those two outflows to the net, and you get back close to the gross. The money never vanished; it was just heading the other way.

## Are foreign investors just taking their profits home?

Yes, and that is a sign of a healthy investment, not a crisis. Repatriation includes both profits and the return of capital when a foreign investor sells. The line on the chart has risen from zero in 2001 to over 51 billion dollars today. That is what happens when a country has a large, mature stock of foreign investment. Profits get earned, and some of them get paid out. India’s FDI stock is larger than it was a decade ago, so repatriation should be larger. Think of it as a dividend cheque, not a flight.

## Has India become a capital exporter?

Quietly, yes. The stock of investment Indian firms hold abroad was $124 million in 1990. By the end of 2024, it was about $260 billion. That is not an annual flow; it is the accumulated value of factories, subsidiaries, and brands Indian companies own around the world. India now exports capital on a scale that would have been unthinkable a generation ago. A two-way capital flow is what maturing economies do.

## How much has Indian investment abroad grown?

The yearly outflow, the money Indian firms sent abroad each year, roughly doubled in five years. It rose from $13 billion in 2019-20 to $28.2 billion in 2024-25. Every dollar an Indian company spends to buy a firm in London or build a plant in Vietnam counts as an outflow that reduces net FDI. That is not a bad thing; it means Indian businesses are competitive enough to go global. But it means the net FDI headline can fall even while India attracts record inflows, simply because its own companies are also investing abroad.

## Why do portfolio flows look so violent month to month?

Because FII is hot money. The monthly chart is a seismograph. In March 2020, when COVID hit, $14.6 billion left in a single month. Eight months later, in November 2020, $10.9 billion flowed in. These are not responses to India’s tax policy or election results. They are capital racing in and out on global fear and greed. A bad month does not mean a broken economy; it means a fund manager in New York hit the sell button. The monthly noise is the whole point.

## What do annual FII swings tell us?

Even the yearly totals are wild. In 2020-21, net FII was $36.1 billion. In 2021-22, it flipped to a negative $16.8 billion. Next year, 2023-24, it bounced back to $44.1 billion. If you only look at one year, you can tell any story you want. The pattern is that there is no pattern. Portfolio investors are not making a long-term bet on India’s institutions; they are trading global conditions. The annual figures confirm that no single year’s number should be read as a verdict.

## Why did equity leave while debt poured in?

Lumping all FII together hides the real story. In 2024-25, foreign portfolio investors sold net equity worth 1,27,041 crore rupees while buying net debt worth 1,43,162 crore rupees. The two arms moved in opposite directions. Equity investors, chasing growth and taking risk, pulled back. Debt investors, seeking stable returns, piled in. This split became dramatic because of a structural event, not sentiment.

## What was the bond-index moment?

In 2024-25, the Fully Accessible Route, a category of government bonds with no foreign investment limits, saw an inflow of 80,691 crore rupees. That single route accounted for more than half of all net debt FPI. The reason was not sudden love for India; it was that global bond indices, like the JP Morgan emerging-market index, had decided to include Indian government bonds. Passive funds that track those indices had to buy. The inflow was mechanical, scripted, and largely one-off. It shows how much portfolio money is driven by global plumbing, not local conviction.

## Does the US dollar really drive FII out of India?

The link is the strongest in the data. When the US dollar strengthens against emerging-market currencies, FII equity flows tend to leave. The correlation is minus 0.37. It is not a law, but it is a consistent tilt. A rising dollar makes Indian rupee assets less attractive to a global investor. The dollar index against EM currencies has moved from 100 in 2006 to 128.63 recently, and many outflow months line up with those surges. Washington, not Delhi, is often the trigger.

## Do US interest rates pull the strings?

Higher US interest rates make safe American bonds pay more. When the US 10-year Treasury yield rises or the Federal Reserve hikes its overnight rate, the pull of safe-haven assets grows. The correlation between FII equity flows and changes in the 10-year yield is minus 0.12, and with the Fed funds rate level it is minus 0.11. These are weaker links than the dollar, but they all point the same way: when the US tightens, money tends to leave emerging markets. The effect is a background hum, not a siren.

## Does global fear sell Indian stocks?

The VIX, often called the fear index, measures expected volatility in US stocks. When it spikes, the world gets scared, and money flees risk. The correlation with monthly FII equity flows is minus 0.33 for the VIX and minus 0.34 for the EM-focused volatility index. During the 2020 COVID crash, the VIX shot to its highest levels and FII exited at record speed. Fear is contagious, and Indian markets catch it.

## What actually moves FII money the most?

When you rank the global forces by their statistical association with FII equity flows, the US dollar against EM currencies comes first at minus 0.37, followed by EM volatility at minus 0.34, the VIX at minus 0.33, the US 10-year yield at minus 0.12, and the Fed funds rate at minus 0.11. All pull in the same direction, stronger dollar, higher fear, higher US rates all correlate with outflows. But these are moderate numbers, not iron laws. Global financial conditions tilt the river, but they do not fully determine the current. A lot of month-to-month noise remains unexplained.

## Where does FDI ‘come from’?

The top sources on a cumulative basis are tiny tax-treaty hubs. Mauritius accounts for $180 billion, about 24.7 percent of all FDI equity since 2000. Singapore is right behind at $175 billion, another 24 percent. The United States, the actual economic superpower, is a distant third at $70.7 billion, just 9.7 percent. Money often routes through Mauritius or Singapore to benefit from tax treaties, so the ‘source country’ on paper is not the true origin. This is a routing story, not a story about island nations being the world’s great investors.

## Who really owns India’s portfolio investments?

When you look at portfolio holdings, the tax-haven pattern nearly vanishes. According to NSDL custody data for May 2026, US-based investors hold 30.8 lakh crore rupees of Indian stocks and bonds, 41.2 percent of all foreign portfolio assets. Mauritius, which dominates the FDI source list, holds just 3.45 lakh crore rupees, a 4.6 percent share. Portfolio money, which is less reliant on tax treaties than direct investments, reveals its true face: it is overwhelmingly American, European, and Singaporean institutional money.

## Which sectors get the foreign direct investment?

The biggest cumulative chunk is services, including finance, banking, and insurance, at $119 billion, 16.3 percent of the total. Computer software and hardware is a close second at $111 billion, 15.2 percent. Together, these two knowledge-economy sectors make up nearly a third of all FDI. Trading, telecom, automobiles, and infrastructure construction trail behind. The data tells an honest story: foreign money came to India for its services and digital economy, not primarily for factories. The ‘Make in India’ manufacturing push accounts for a noticeably smaller share.

## Is India’s share of world FDI really shrinking?

India’s slice of the global FDI pie has never been large. It climbed from 0.12 percent in 1990 to around 2 percent in recent years. In 2024, it stood at 1.83 percent. The recent dip is partly a global story: total world FDI itself contracted in some years, so India’s share can wobble. The chart shows that India has hovered in this 1 to 3 percent band for decades. It is a small, steady piece of a big and volatile pie.

## How does India compare with peer economies?

In 2024, India attracted $27.6 billion in FDI inflows. The United States drew $279 billion, ten times as much. Singapore, a city-state, pulled in $143 billion. China got $116 billion, and Brazil $59.2 billion. Even Mexico, at $36.9 billion, was ahead. India’s number is not large for its economic size, and a single year’s figure must be read with caution, one big deal can skew it. But the ranking over many years shows India still punches below its weight in attracting the patient money that builds lasting assets.

chartExplainers.title: The number everyone is panicking about
chartExplainers.takeaway: Net FDI fell from $$43 billion in FY20 to just $about $1 billion in FY25, a collapse that made headlines worldwide.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows the annual net foreign direct investment in US dollars from FY2001 to FY2025. Net FDI is what remains after subtracting repatriation and outward investment from gross inflows. The line climbs slowly, jumps to a peak of $$43 billion in 2019-20, and then plunges to $about $1 billion. That visual cliff is what every newsroom quoted. But the net figure is not a measure of fresh money coming in; it is the result of a subtraction. Reading it as a stand-alone number without the outflows is like judging a household's income by looking only at the savings account balance after all bills are paid. The real story lies in the flows that made the net number shrink.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To confront the alarming headline number head-on and show the magnitude of the decline that caused the panic.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The line shows annual net FDI in US$ million. Notice the sharp drop after the 2019-20 peak.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume this line by itself tells you whether foreigners increased or decreased their investment in India.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use large labels and sparse x-axis ticks so the drop is clear on a small screen.

chartExplainers.title: Patient money and hot money
chartExplainers.takeaway: FDI is steady patient money; FII swings wildly from +$$36.1 billion one year to –$$16.8 billion the next.
chartExplainers.detail: Two lines share the same axis: net FDI and net portfolio (FII/FPI) investment. FDI moves like a slow hill, rising and falling gently over decades. Portfolio flows spike and crash. In 2020-21, net FII raced to $$36.1 billion. The very next year it plunged to –$$16.8 billion. FDI barely budged. This chart is the simplest proof that FDI and FII are entirely different kinds of money. FDI builds factories; FII trades stocks. The data come from the RBI's balance of payments and are both net figures, so they are directly comparable.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To visually separate the two concepts of foreign money and show why confusing them leads to wrong panic.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Two lines with the same scale; the volatile one is FII, the stable one is FDI.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume a sudden drop in one line means the other also changed.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Limit to two lines; colour-code clearly and label only key peaks and troughs.

chartExplainers.title: Gross inflows hit a record the year net 'collapsed'
chartExplainers.takeaway: Gross FDI inflows reached an all-time high of $$80.6 billion in FY2024-25, the very year net fell to under $1 billion.
chartExplainers.detail: This dual-line chart shows gross FDI inflows and net FDI together. Gross inflows climbed from $$4.0 billion in 2001 to a record $$80.6 billion in 2024-25. Meanwhile, net FDI fell from its peak. The two lines, which once moved together, have parted dramatically since 2019-20. The distance between them is the sum of money flowing out. The chart is the single most important visual for correcting the misreading. Foreigners did not stop coming; they came in larger numbers than ever. The panic was about the wrong number.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To reveal the central myth-buster: the inflow tap was wide open even as net collapsed.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The blue line (gross) goes up and to the right; the orange line (net) peels away and declines.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read the falling line as falling inflows; it is the net result of larger outflows.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep the two lines distinct with strong colour contrast and highlight the record year data point.

chartExplainers.title: What eats the gap: repatriation and Indians investing abroad
chartExplainers.takeaway: In FY2024-25, outflows from repatriation ($$51.5 billion) and outward FDI ($$28.2 billion) consumed almost all the record gross inflow.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart deconstructs net FDI. It stacks gross inflows at the top, then subtracts repatriation and outward FDI to arrive at net. The two subtractions have grown dramatically. Repatriation rose from $$18.4 billion in FY20 to $$51.5 billion; outward FDI from $$13 billion to $$28.2 billion. In FY2024-25, the two drains together exceeded $79 billion, almost exactly matching the gross inflow. The net that remained was under $1 billion. The visual makes the arithmetic transparent: net FDI didn't disappear; it was paid out.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To show the exact components that chipped away the net and demonstrate that the gap is not mysterious.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the stacked bars or lines: top is gross, then two outflows, then net at the bottom.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat repatriation as a sign of distress; it includes normal profit remittances.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: If bars, keep them wide enough; if lines, use distinct colours and maybe a shaded area between gross and net.

chartExplainers.title: Foreign investors are taking profits home
chartExplainers.takeaway: Repatriation nearly tripled from $$18.4 billion in FY20 to $$51.5 billion in FY25.
chartExplainers.detail: This single-line chart tracks annual repatriation and disinvestment. Twenty years ago, the figure was zero. It has climbed steadily, reflecting the growing stock of foreign investment in India. Older investments mature and start paying dividends or get sold, sending money back. The line's steep rise after 2019-20 is the single largest reason net FDI fell. Think of it as a factory that was built a decade ago finally generating enough cash to send profits back to its parent. That is a sign the investment worked, not that the investor is fleeing.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To isolate the largest drain and explain that it is a normal feature of a maturing FDI stock.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A line climbing from near zero to over $51 billion; focus on the sharp rise in recent years.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not equate repatriation only with disinvestment panic; much of it is profit distribution.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Show the increasing line with a clear y-axis and label the latest value.

chartExplainers.title: India has quietly become a capital exporter
chartExplainers.takeaway: The stock of investment Indian firms hold abroad stands at $$260 billion, up from $$124 million in 1990.
chartExplainers.detail: This UNCTAD chart shows India's outward FDI stock over three decades. The line starts flat near zero in 1990, then arcs upward after the 2000s. It crosses $100 billion around 2010 and surpasses $260 billion by 2024. This is the accumulated value of Indian-owned factories, brands, and subsidiaries around the world. It means Indian companies have become net investors abroad. This long-term transformation is a fundamental shift: India is no longer just a destination for foreign capital; it is a source as well. That changes how we must read the FDI numbers.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To show the scale and historical arc of India's emergence as a capital exporter.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A long-run line curving upward; note the acceleration after 2005.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This is a stock, not an annual flow; stock values accumulate and don't reset each year.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a smooth line with key milestones labelled (e.g., $1bn, $100bn, $260bn).

chartExplainers.title: And the yearly outflow has doubled
chartExplainers.takeaway: Annual outward FDI by Indian companies rose from $$13 billion in FY20 to $$28.2 billion in FY25.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart zooms in on the yearly flow, not the stock. The RBI data shows outward direct investment rising from under $1 billion in the early 2000s to $28.17 billion in the latest year. The steep climb in the last five years is what directly ate into net FDI. Every dollar an Indian conglomerate spends to acquire a foreign company counts as an outflow that reduces the net figure. This is not capital flight; it is Indian business going global, a pattern seen earlier in South Korea and China at similar stages of development.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To show the recent acceleration of Indian outward investment as a key factor shrinking net FDI.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Line chart; notice the steep post-2019 rise and label the doubling from FY20 to FY25.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not interpret all outward FDI as new greenfield investment; some may be round-tripping or financial engineering.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep the line clean, highlight the FY2024-25 value, and add a light annotation showing the 5-year increase.

chartExplainers.title: Hot money, month by month
chartExplainers.takeaway: Monthly net FII swings from an outflow of –$$14.6 billion (March 2020) to an inflow of $$10.9 billion (November 2020) in the same year.
chartExplainers.detail: This monthly line chart from RBI shows net portfolio investment since 2011. The line is a jagged sawtooth. March 2020, when COVID hit, recorded a record outflow of $$14.6 billion. By November, as markets rebounded, $$10.9 billion poured back in. No factory opens or closes that fast. This is hot money: buying and selling by global funds that can reverse direction in days. The chart is noisy, and that is its entire point. A bad month does not mean a bad economy; it means fund managers shifted their bets.

chartExplainers.howToRead: Look for the extreme spikes; the y-axis will need to handle both large negative and positive values.

chartExplainers.mobileNote: Sparse monthly ticks on x-axis; label only the extreme months to avoid clutter.

chartExplainers.title: Three wild years in a row
chartExplainers.takeaway: Annual net FII swung from $$36.1 billion (FY21) to –$$16.8 billion (FY22) to $$44.1 billion (FY24).
chartExplainers.detail: This bar chart simplifies the volatility to annual totals. Even when you smooth out the months, the numbers lurch. A $53 billion swing in two years, followed by a $60 billion reversal, is extreme. This is not the steady behavior of patient money. It reflects global liquidity waves, risk appetite, and interest rate cycles. The bars show that no single year's FII number should be read as a referendum on India's policies. The money comes and goes on global tides.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To show that even annual aggregation does not dampen the violent swings of portfolio flows.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Three bars, one per fiscal year, alternating between positive and negative; heights in billions.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume the most recent year's number is a new normal; FII does not have a normal.

chartExplainers.title: Equity walked out while debt poured in
chartExplainers.takeaway: In FY2024-25, net equity FPI was –₹1,27,041 crore while net debt FPI was +₹1,43,162 crore.
chartExplainers.detail: This dual-line chart uses NSDL depository data in rupees to split portfolio flows into equity and debt. The two lines move in opposite directions in the most recent year. Equity, the riskier bet, saw a heavy exodus. Debt, the safer asset, attracted strong inflows. This split is invisible in the headline FII number. It tells us that the sell-off was not a blanket rejection of India; it was a reallocation from stocks to bonds. The drivers were different: equity flows respond to growth fears and currency swings, while debt flows responded to a structural index inclusion.

chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are NSDL depository transaction figures in rupees; do not directly compare to RBI BoP dollar figures.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep the two lines distinct; label the latest divergence clearly in a callout.

chartExplainers.title: The bond-index moment
chartExplainers.takeaway: Debt inflows via the Fully Accessible Route surged to ₹80,691 crore in FY2024-25, a one-off structural event.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart shows net FPI debt under the FAR route. For years, the line was flat near zero. Then, in FY2024-25, it shot up to ₹80,691 crore. That is not because foreign investors suddenly fell in love with Indian bonds; it is because global bond indices included Indian government securities, and the FAR was the channel. Passive funds that track those indices had to buy. This inflow was mechanical and likely non-recurring. It explains why debt inflows were so strong even as equity investors fled.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To show that a large part of recent debt FPI was scripted by index inclusion, not sentiment.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A line that stays near zero for most of the chart, then spikes dramatically in the latest year.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not expect this exact level of FAR inflow to repeat every year; it was a one-time adjustment by index-trackers.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a clear annotation callout on the spike explaining the bond-index trigger.

chartExplainers.title: The real trigger sits in Washington
chartExplainers.takeaway: The US dollar index against EM currencies correlates at –0.37 with monthly FII equity flows, the strongest link.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart from the Fed shows the dollar’s value against a basket of emerging-market currencies. When the line rises, the dollar strengthens, making rupee assets less attractive. The visual often shows a rise in the dollar index during months when FII equity outflows accelerate. The statistical correlation is –0.37, meaning the relationship is consistent over many months. It is not a perfect predictor, some dollar surges coincide with smaller outflows, but it is the most powerful global variable in the dataset. When the dollar strengthens, hot money tends to leave India.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To establish the dollar as the most important external driver of FII flows.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A line chart of the index; look for periods of sharp rise that coincide with known outflow months.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Correlation does not mean the dollar alone caused each outflow; other factors are always at play.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep the line clean; annotate a couple of major dollar spikes with their corresponding outflow months.

chartExplainers.title: The US rate cycle pulls the strings
chartExplainers.takeaway: Higher US 10-year yields and Fed funds rates correlate with FII outflows, though weakly (around –0.12).
chartExplainers.detail: Two lines track US interest rates: the 10-year Treasury yield and the Federal Reserve’s overnight rate. Both rose sharply in recent years as the Fed fought inflation. When US rates go up, global investors can earn more by parking money in safe US bonds, reducing the appeal of Indian stocks. The correlation numbers are modest: –0.12 for the yield and –0.11 for the fed funds rate. That means the link is there but it is a background factor, not a daily trigger. Rate cycles set the environment in which hot money moves, but they don’t dictate every gyration.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To show the interest-rate channel that subtly pulls capital away from emerging markets.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Two lines with the same percent axis; both trend upward in recent years, with the Fed funds rate lagging the yield.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume a rate hike causes an immediate outflow; the correlation is weak and indirect.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Overlay both lines with clear labels; annotate the recent peak and mention the correlation.

chartExplainers.title: When the world gets scared, India gets sold
chartExplainers.takeaway: The VIX (global fear index) and EM-VIX both spike during crisis months when FII flees; correlation is about –0.33.
chartExplainers.detail: Two volatility indices, the VIX and the EM-VIX, measure expected market turmoil. When they spike, it signals panic. The chart shows that during the 2020 COVID crash, both indices shot to record highs just as India recorded its worst monthly FII outflow. The correlation with FII equity flows is –0.33 for the VIX and –0.34 for the EM-VIX. Fear is a powerful driver: when global investors get scared, they sell what they perceive as risky, and Indian equities fall into that bucket. The chart makes that risk-off behavior visible.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To visually connect spikes in global fear with episodes of FII selling in India.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Two lines (VIX and EM-VIX) often move together; spikes correspond to shaded outflow months.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The VIX is a US-centric measure; EM-VIX is more specific to emerging markets but both are imperfect.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a shared index axis, maybe shade the 2020 crisis period for clarity.

chartExplainers.title: What actually moves FII money
chartExplainers.takeaway: The dollar is the strongest pull (–0.37), followed by EM volatility (–0.34), VIX (–0.33), US yield (–0.12), and Fed rate (–0.11).
chartExplainers.detail: This horizontal bar chart ranks the correlation of each global factor with monthly FII equity flows. All bars point left (negative), meaning each factor is associated with outflows when it strengthens. The longest bar is the dollar at –0.37, then EM volatility at –0.34, then the VIX, then the yield and the Fed rate. The differences are not huge, but the pattern is unanimous: global tightening and fear tilt the odds in favor of outflows. The chart is clear: Delhi politics is not the main character; the global weather is.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To summarize the relative pulling power of global conditions on FII equity flows.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Bars extending left from a zero line; longer bars mean stronger negative correlation.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are correlations, not causation; they measure association, not what caused each monthly move.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars with labels inside or right-aligned; sort from strongest to weakest.

chartExplainers.title: FDI 'comes from' tiny tax-treaty hubs
chartExplainers.takeaway: Mauritius ($$180 billion, 24.7%) and Singapore ($$175 billion, 24%) account for nearly half of cumulative FDI equity.
chartExplainers.detail: This DPIIT bar chart shows the source of cumulative FDI equity since 2000. Mauritius and Singapore tower over every other country. The United States, at $$70.7 billion (9.7%), is a distant third. These small jurisdictions are not the ultimate origin of the money; they are treaty-routing hubs. Investors often channel funds through them to benefit from double-taxation avoidance agreements. So the chart is a map of legal structures, not a map of where the beneficial owners actually live. It’s a reminder that the headline source of FDI can be a financial address, not a home country.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To reveal the tax-treaty routing that distorts the stated origin of direct investment into India.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Horizontal bars sorted by share; Mauritius and Singapore dominate, US is smaller.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This is cumulative since 2000 and equity only; do not read it as the current year's flow or the true beneficial ownership.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Show top 5-6 countries as bars; include share percentages next to the bar labels.

chartExplainers.title: But portfolio money is real American money
chartExplainers.takeaway: US-based investors hold 41.2% of all FPI assets in India (₹30.8 lakh crore); Mauritius holds only 4.6% (₹3.45 lakh crore).
chartExplainers.detail: This NSDL custody bar chart flips the lens. Now, the US dominates, with total assets under custody of ₹30.8 lakh crore. Luxembourg, Ireland, and the UK follow. Mauritius, which topped the FDI chart, shrinks to just ₹3.45 lakh crore, a 4.6 percent share. Portfolio investment, which is largely publicly traded securities, has little benefit from tax treaties, so it reveals its true national origin. The chart confirms that much of the real money behind India’s markets is American, with European and Japanese funds also significant. The tax-haven pattern of FDI is almost entirely absent.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To contrast the true geographic origin of portfolio holdings with the tax-routing pattern of FDI.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Horizontal bars sorted by total assets; US is far and away the largest, Mauritius is small.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This is a stock snapshot from May 2026; it reflects holdings, not recent flows.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Show top 5-7 countries; label US and Mauritius with their shares to highlight the contrast.

chartExplainers.title: And it goes into services, not factories
chartExplainers.takeaway: Services (₹$119 billion, 16.3%) and computer software (₹$111 billion, 15.2%) are the largest cumulative FDI sectors.
chartExplainers.detail: This DPIIT bar chart shows where cumulative FDI equity has landed by sector. Services, a broad category including finance and banking, and computer software together account for nearly a third. Trading, telecom, and automobiles are next, with manufacturing sectors like drugs and chemicals further down. The picture is clear: foreign direct investors came for India's digital, financial, and services growth, not primarily to build factories. The 'Make in India' vision has attracted some capital, but the money has overwhelmingly backed the knowledge economy. This sectoral skew is a structural feature, not a recent twist.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To show the sectoral destination of FDI and challenge the manufacturing narrative.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Horizontal bars; services and software are the tallest, far ahead of traditional manufacturing sectors.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Sector categories are broad; 'services' includes many sub-sectors that DPIIT does not split here.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Show top 7-8 sectors; add share percentages and group by service vs manufacturing visually.

chartExplainers.title: India is a small slice of world FDI
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's share of global FDI inflows was 1.83% in 2024, never having exceeded 3% historically.
chartExplainers.detail: This UNCTAD line chart shows India's percentage of world FDI inflows since 1990. The line crawls from near zero to around 2 percent. It dips during global slowdowns, the 2008 crisis, the pandemic, and rises in boom years. But it never breaks out. That means India's absolute FDI numbers move largely with the global tide. When world FDI shrinks, India's drops, even if no policy has changed. A low percentage doesn't mean the money is insignificant, but it does mean India is a small part of a big picture. The recent dip is partly a global story.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To right-size India's FDI inflows in the context of global capital flows.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A horizontal line that oscillates between 0% and 3%; focus on its stability, not its wiggles.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Share can fall even if India's absolute inflows rise, if the rest of the world grows faster.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep the line simple with a few reference years labelled; the range is small so use a full y-axis.

chartExplainers.title: Still well behind the leaders
chartExplainers.takeaway: In 2024, India's FDI inflow was $$27.6 billion, far below the US ($$279 billion), Singapore, China, and Brazil.
chartExplainers.detail: This bar chart uses UNCTAD data to rank selected economies by FDI inflow in 2024. The US towers at $278.8 billion. Singapore, a city-state, drew $143.4 billion, and China $116.2 billion. Brazil attracted $59.2 billion, and Mexico $36.9 billion. India, at $27.6 billion, is nearer the bottom of this peer set. For an economy of its size, India's FDI numbers are modest. A single year can be skewed by one big deal, but the multi-year pattern is that India attracts less than one might expect. The chart is a reality check against the idea that India is a top destination for long-term investment.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: To benchmark India's FDI inflows against key emerging and developed economies and highlight the gap.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Horizontal bars in descending order; US and Singapore far outstrip the rest; India is near the bottom.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: A single year's figure can be distorted; compare multi-year trends for a fuller picture.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Label each bar with the country and value; maybe use a log scale if the range is too wide but preference is linear with broken axis or simple annotation.

editorialPlanDraft.answerThesis: India’s net foreign direct investment fell to a trickle in 2024-25 even as gross inflows hit a record high; the collapse was driven by surging repatriation and Indian outward investment, not by foreigners abandoning India. Meanwhile, volatile portfolio flows are steered more by global monetary conditions and risk appetite than by domestic politics.
requiredConcepts: The central myth-buster: Net FDI fell from ~$43bn (FY20) to ~$1bn (FY25), but gross inflows rose to a record ~$81bn. Net collapsed because outflows grew (repatriation ~$18bn to ~$51bn, outward FDI ~$13bn to ~$28bn). Reading net as gross is the biggest mistake.
FDI (10%+ stake, lasting control, patient money) vs FII/FPI (portfolio, no control, hot money). Recorded separately in the balance of payments and behave completely differently.
Why the net FDI number fell: repatriation nearly tripled, outward FDI roughly doubled, while gross inflows held at a record. Near-zero net FDI is partly a sign of maturity, not flight.

Why a flow can turn negative: repatriation is normal and rises as past investments mature; disinvestment and portfolio exits happen when global conditions shift. Negative months are normal capital-flow behaviour.
India has quietly become a capital exporter. Outward FDI stock grew from ~$1.7bn (2000) to ~$260bn (2024, UNCTAD). Annual outward flow roughly doubled from ~$13bn (FY20) to ~$28bn (FY25).
The FII rollercoaster: net portfolio investment swung from ~$36bn (FY21) to –$17bn (FY22) to ~$44bn (FY24). Monthly volatility is extreme: –$14.6bn (Mar 2020 COVID shock) to +$11bn (Nov 2020).

Not all FII is alike: equity and debt often move in opposite directions. In FY2024-25, foreigners sold net equity of ₹1.27 lakh crore while buying net debt of ₹1.43 lakh crore, with ~₹80,691 crore via the Fully Accessible Route (FAR).

Where FDI goes (DPIIT cumulative equity): services (finance etc., ~$119bn, 16%) and computer software/hardware (~$111bn, 15%) dominate; manufacturing draws a noticeably smaller share. Foreign money chased the digital and services economy.

What moves FII money: monthly equity flows are negatively correlated with the US dollar vs EM (–0.37), EM volatility (–0.34), VIX (–0.33), US 10-year yield (–0.12), Fed funds rate (–0.11). A one-point rise in the EM dollar index is associated with ~$840mn equity outflows. These are moderate tilts, not laws; correlation ≠ causation.

The tax-haven puzzle: On a DPIIT cumulative basis, Mauritius (~$180bn, ~25%) and Singapore (~$175bn, ~24%) are the top FDI sources. For FPI custody (NSDL, May 2026), the US alone holds ~41% of assets (₹30.8 lakh crore), while Mauritius is under 5%. FDI routes through treaty hubs; portfolio money reveals its true origin.

The global lens: India’s share of world FDI inflows is usually 2–3% (1.83% in 2024, UNCTAD). In 2024, FDI inflows: US $279bn, Singapore $143bn, China $116bn, Brazil $59bn, India $27.6bn. Swings in the global total move India’s number a lot; a single year is volatile.

Methodology honesty: Never mix four different datasets: RBI BoP (gross/net/repatriation, fiscal years), NSDL depository (equity/debt FII in ₹), DPIIT (cumulative FDI by source, stock since 2000), UNCTAD (global comparison, calendar years). Gross ≠ net; commitments ≠ flows; assets under custody are a stock; CDSL and NSDL must not be added.

chartPlan.title: The number everyone is panicking about
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Net FDI fell from about $43bn (FY20) to under $1bn (FY25). Every headline screams this.
chartPlan.howToRead: Line chart shows annual net FDI in US$ million. Focus on the sharp drop after the 2019-20 peak.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read this as proof that foreigners stopped investing; it is only the net after outflows.

chartPlan.title: Patient money and hot money
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The two kinds of foreign money behave completely differently.
chartPlan.howToRead: Two lines: net FDI (steady) vs net FPI/FII (volatile). Even at annual frequency, FII swings wildly.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume FDI and FII respond to the same triggers.

chartPlan.title: Gross inflows hit a record the year net 'collapsed'
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Foreigners did not stop coming. Gross inflows actually rose to a record ~$81bn.
chartPlan.howToRead: Blue line (gross inflows) shows a rising trend, with the highest point in FY2024-25. The net FDI line (orange) falls.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't confuse gross (money coming in) with net (money staying).

chartPlan.title: What eats the gap: repatriation and Indians investing abroad
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Net = gross minus repatriation minus outward FDI. Both subtractions grew.
chartPlan.howToRead: Stacked view: gross inflows at top, then repatriation and outward FDI as negative bars, net FDI as the result.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't treat repatriation only as an exit; it often reflects profitable operations.

chartPlan.title: Foreign investors are taking profits home
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Repatriation and disinvestment are why a flow turns negative, and they are rising.
chartPlan.howToRead: Line chart showing repatriation climbing from ~$18bn (FY20) to ~$51bn (FY25).
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Rising repatriation does not always mean panic; much of it is normal profit distribution.

chartPlan.title: India has quietly become a capital exporter
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Indian firms now hold a large and growing stock of investments abroad.
chartPlan.howToRead: Line chart from 1990: outward FDI stock starts near zero and shoots up to ~$260bn by 2024.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Stock values are not annual flows; they accumulate over decades.

chartPlan.title: And the yearly outflow has doubled
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The annual pace of Indian investment abroad roughly doubled in five years.
chartPlan.howToRead: Line chart showing annual outward FDI flow; note the steep rise after FY2019-20.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Part of this may be round-tripping (money that returns to India through Mauritius/Singapore).

chartPlan.title: Hot money, month by month
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Portfolio flows are violent at monthly resolution, which is the point of 'hot money'.
chartPlan.howToRead: Line chart of monthly net FII; look for extreme swings like March 2020 (–$14.6bn) and November 2020 (+$10.9bn).
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't over-interpret a single month; it's the pattern that matters.

chartPlan.title: Three wild years in a row
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Even annually, FII swings between large inflows and outflows.
chartPlan.howToRead: Bar chart of annual net FII for the last three fiscal years: +$36bn, –$17bn, +$44bn.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Annual figures can hide the intra-year chaos; FII is inherently volatile.

chartPlan.title: Equity walked out while debt poured in
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Lumping 'FII' together hides that equity and debt often move in opposite directions.
chartPlan.howToRead: Two lines: net equity (red, falling) and net debt (green, rising) in FY2024-25.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: These are NSDL depository figures in rupees; they are not identical to RBI BoP dollar flows.

chartPlan.title: The bond-index moment
chartPlan.whyShowThis: A structural event, not sentiment, drove the recent debt inflows.
chartPlan.howToRead: Line chart showing net FPI debt under FAR; a steep jump in FY2024-25 to ₹80,691 crore.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: FAR is a subset of all debt inflows; bond-index flows may not repeat every year.

chartPlan.title: The real trigger sits in Washington
chartPlan.whyShowThis: When the dollar strengthens against emerging-market currencies, money leaves India.
chartPlan.howToRead: Line chart of the US dollar index vs EM currencies; upward trend often coincides with FII outflows.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Correlation is –0.37, meaning the dollar explains some but not all of the movement.

chartPlan.title: The US rate cycle pulls the strings
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Higher US rates make safe US assets more attractive than emerging-market risk.
chartPlan.howToRead: Dual-line chart of US 10-year yield and Fed funds rate; rises often precede FII outflows.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: The correlation with FII flows is weak (–0.12 for yields, –0.11 for Fed funds); rates are a background factor.

chartPlan.title: When the world gets scared, India gets sold
chartPlan.whyShowThis: FII is risk-on/risk-off money; spikes in global fear coincide with outflows.
chartPlan.howToRead: Overlay of VIX and EM-VIX; both spike during crises when FII flees.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: VIX measures implied volatility of US stocks; EM-VIX is more relevant but less liquid.

chartPlan.title: What actually moves FII money
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Putting the global drivers side by side: all of them pull the same way.
chartPlan.howToRead: Horizontal bar chart of correlation coefficients; all negative, with the dollar leading at –0.37.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: These are correlations of month-over-month changes; they don't imply causation.

chartPlan.title: FDI 'comes from' tiny tax-treaty hubs
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Two small jurisdictions account for nearly half of India's cumulative FDI.
chartPlan.howToRead: Bar chart of cumulative FDI equity by source country; Mauritius and Singapore dwarf others.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: DPIIT data is cumulative since 2000 and equity-only; these are not annual flows or the ultimate beneficial ownership.

chartPlan.title: But portfolio money is real American money
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Flip to portfolio holdings and the tax-haven pattern vanishes.
chartPlan.howToRead: Bar chart of FPI assets under custody by country; US dominates at ₹30.8 lakh crore (41%), Mauritius at ₹3.45 lakh crore (4.6%).
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Custody data reflects holdings (stock), not recent flows; country of custody is not always the beneficial owner.

chartPlan.title: And it goes into services, not factories
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Where the money lands is as revealing as where it comes from.
chartPlan.howToRead: Bar chart of cumulative FDI by sector; services and software together account for about a third.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Sector categories are broad; 'services' includes everything from consulting to banking.

chartPlan.title: India is a small slice of world FDI
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Zoom out and India's recent dip is partly a global FDI slowdown, not just India's.
chartPlan.howToRead: Line chart of India's share of world FDI inflows; never above 3%, with dips during global downturns.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Share can fall even when absolute inflows rise if the rest of the world grows faster.

chartPlan.title: Still well behind the leaders
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Against peers, India attracts less FDI than its size might suggest.
chartPlan.howToRead: Bar chart of 2024 FDI inflows for selected economies; US at top, India at $27.6bn, well below Brazil and Mexico.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: A single year can be skewed; trend over a decade is more meaningful.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Money a foreign entity invests to gain lasting control – typically a 10% stake or more – in an Indian business. Think of it as building a factory or buying a company. It's 'patient' money that stays for years.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The entire panic is about FDI's net figure; understanding the difference from portfolio flows is essential.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Money foreign investors put into Indian shares, bonds, or other financial assets on the open market without seeking control. It's 'hot' money that can be sold and pulled out overnight.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: FII drives the monthly volatility; it behaves completely differently from FDI.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Gross FDI is the total money coming in. Net FDI is what remains after subtracting money that leaves (repatriation, outward investment). A fall in net does not mean gross fell.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The central myth-buster of the whole page.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Profits, dividends, or the original investment sent back to the foreign investor's home country. It's a normal part of doing business, not a signal of doom, and rises as past investments mature.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Repatriation is the biggest reason net FDI fell, and it's partly a sign of success.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Money Indian companies invest abroad to buy or build businesses. Tata Motors buying Jaguar Land Rover is an example. It counts as an outflow in the FDI account.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Indian outward investment roughly doubled in five years, directly reducing net FDI.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A country's financial ledger recording all money flows in and out. It has a current account (trade, services) and a capital account (FDI, FII, loans). FDI and FII are recorded in the capital account.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The RBI data we use comes from the BoP; it's the official scorecard.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A special category of Indian government bonds where foreign investors face no limits on how much they can buy. It was created partly to get Indian bonds into global bond indices.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Most of the debt inflow in 2024-25 came through FAR, showing it was index-driven.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The total value of securities that a depository (like NSDL) holds on behalf of foreign investors. It's a stock measure – a snapshot of what they own, not what they bought that year.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The FPI-by-country chart uses AUC to show who holds Indian stocks and bonds.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A real-time market index that represents the market's expectation of 30-day forward-looking volatility. Often called the 'fear gauge'. When it spikes, global investors flee risky assets.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: VIX movements correlate with FII outflows, showing hot money reacts to fear.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A Federal Reserve index measuring the value of the US dollar against a basket of emerging-market currencies. When it rises, the dollar is strengthening, making EM assets less attractive.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The strongest correlation with FII equity flows; a rising dollar pulls money out.
